name: Colin Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Colin. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI firms, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be named. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I'm a marketing specialist at Paddock Pet Foods, a dog and cat food brand. Most days I'm at my desk planning promotions with pet shops and supermarkets: the price deals, the brochures we send to shop buyers, and the loyalty emails to pet owners. Twice a month I drive out to the bigger shops to check our displays and chat with the managers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the shop visits most. You learn more in ten minutes chatting with a shop manager about what owners are actually buying than in a week of reports. What gets to me is the money: I live alone in a small flat, I'm paying off the car I need for those visits, and I've got about three weeks of money saved. There aren't many marketing jobs near here, so I can't afford to be picky.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I use one to tidy up the brochure text and to sum up long sales reports. I didn't touch it until my manager, Rob, showed us it actually saved time. I'm not a first-in kind of person, but I'm not a holdout either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair enough. That's roughly how I'd have guessed it, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent helper and not much more, which is what I'd have said anyway. At the pub I'd say the people who panicked look a bit silly now. I wouldn't post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job's probably safe, but my life's still tight. The car loan has two years left and my rent went up in the summer. Even without any AI drama, one bad month knocks me sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the tool for the dull parts, like summing up reports. I'd pay off the car loan faster, maybe an extra fifty a month, so that's gone before anything else goes wrong. I'd ask Rob about a small pay rise at my review in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit fed up that money's tight whether the world changes or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the car's clutch went, and the repair was about a month's rent. I put it on a credit card and it took me half a year to clear. I'd like to never do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change, in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like more of the shop visits and less of the desk. I'd ask Rob if I could take on more of the field side. It's the part I'm actually good at.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent helper**, nothing more.
At the pub I'd say people who **panicked** look a bit silly now.
think: I think my **job's safe**, but my money's still tight.
A **car loan** and a rent rise mean one bad month knocks me sideways.
do: Use the tool for **dull tasks** like summing up reports.
Pay an **extra fifty** a month off the car loan.
Ask my manager Rob for a **small rise** in March.
feel: I feel **fine, mostly**, but fed up that money's tight anyway.
S0.quote: Last year the car's clutch went, and the repair was about a month's rent.
fieldNote: His pressure is **money**, not AI: a car loan and thin savings.
He'd prefer more **shop visits**, where he feels most useful.
He's measured and **unshowy**, and wouldn't post about it.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to sum up sales reports
Pay an extra fifty a month off the car loan
Ask Rob to take on more of the shop visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing, planning, buying. That's a fair bit of my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the way things are going and we should get on with it. I'd tell the lads at football that you've got to learn this stuff, even if you don't like it. I wouldn't blame anyone in particular.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think half my desk job goes to the software. The brochures, the emails, the deal sums, the AI could do most of it. The AI can't stand in a shop and chat with a manager about why the puppy food isn't selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company AI course once it was proven, and get properly good at the bits I use. I'd go to Rob and pitch myself as the person who handles the shops, the field side, since that's what's left. I'd keep paying down the car and stop eating out, so I'd have a month or two saved if things went wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be okay if I play it right, but I don't love that word if.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Rob says there's no field job, just fewer desk jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd start looking at sales rep jobs with other pet brands, even if it meant more driving. Reps visit shops all day. That's the bit of my job that feels most human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Paddock would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jess, who does our social posts. She's only been there a year, and her whole job is the kind of writing the AI is good at. I'd tell her to get close to the customer side quickly.

say: I'd say it's the **way things are going** and get on with it.
I'd tell friends to **learn the tools**, without blaming anyone.
think: I think **half my desk job** goes to software.
AI can't stand in a shop and **chat with a manager**.
do: Take the **company AI course** once it's proven.
Pitch myself to Rob as the **field person** for shops.
Stop eating out and **build a month** of savings.
feel: I feel **anxious**, because being okay depends on **playing it right**.
S1.quote: The AI can't stand in a shop and chat with a manager about why the puppy food isn't selling.
fieldNote: He expects **half his desk work** to go, and plans to move toward the field.
His adaptability is **steady**: learn once proven, then commit.
He worries for a **newer colleague** whose work is all writing.

steps.text: Take Paddock's AI course once colleagues show it works
Pitch to Rob for a field role visiting pet shops
Stop eating out to build a month of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's quick. That's before the car's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious and the government needs a plan. I'd say firms shouldn't just dump people overnight. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2028 even the shop visits go, because the AI can talk to shop buyers by email and video and set every deal itself. The robots come about 2031, so for a few years the only jobs left are the ones where you use your hands. I'd be out with three weeks of money and a car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the car the moment the job looked shaky and clear the loan. I'd ask my parents if I could move back home for a bit, because they've got the spare room. I'd look for driving or warehouse work, delivery maybe, and get whatever government help there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground moving under the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back home at 27. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty rubbish, honestly. My dad would be fine about it. Moving back home at 27 would feel like going backwards, but it's better than drowning in rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you sold the car, how would you get to delivery work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good point. I'd have to pick a job I can cycle to, or a delivery firm with vans. That's the kind of thing you don't think about until it happens.

say: I'd say it's **serious** and the government needs a plan.
I'd say firms shouldn't **dump people** overnight, calmly but clearly.
think: I think even **the shop visits** go by 2028.
I'd be out with **three weeks** of money and a car loan.
do: Sell the **car** and clear the loan if the job looks shaky.
Move back to my **parents' spare room**.
Look for **delivery or warehouse** work and claim help.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, like the ground's moving under the flat.
S2.quote: Moving back home at 27 would feel like going backwards, but it's better than drowning in rent.
fieldNote: Fast AGI takes even the **face-to-face** part he counted on.
His first moves are **defensive**: sell the car, move home.
He spots a gap only when asked: no car means **fewer jobs** he can reach.

steps.text: Sell the car and clear the loan if the job looks shaky
Move into his parents' spare room
Apply for van delivery or warehouse jobs he can reach

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 32. Okay, that's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it, so businesses and government should work out retraining now. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the desk side of my job goes around 2031. The robots come about 2034, so anything hands-on and with people gives me a few more years. I'd want to see which way things go before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Paddock for a year or two, learn the tools and clear the car loan. I'd watch what jobs people like me move into. I've coached under-tens football on Saturdays for years, so I'd look at a sports coaching qualification, maybe part-time from year two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had a bit of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why coaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coaching under-tens football is the best part of my week, and I come home in a better mood than I ever do from the office. The kids are loud and chaotic, but it's people and it's on a pitch, which I don't see a computer doing soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does coaching pay enough to live on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first, I'd guess. I'd probably need to mix it with something else, like school sports clubs or some sales. I'd have to look into it properly.

say: I'd say businesses and government should **plan retraining** now.
I'd keep it **practical**, talk about what helps, and avoid blaming anyone in particular.
think: I think my **desk work** goes around 2031.
Hands-on work **with people** gives me a few more years, until robots arrive.
do: Stay at Paddock, **learn the tools** and clear the car loan.
Watch where people like me **find work** for a year.
Start a part-time **coaching qualification** from year two.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but with a bit of a plan.
S3.quote: Coaching under-tens football is the best part of my week, and I come home in a better mood than I ever do from the office.
fieldNote: He'd use the extra time to **watch first**, then move.
His Saturday **football coaching** becomes a possible new career.
He's honest that coaching may **not pay enough** on its own.

steps.text: Clear the car loan while staying at Paddock
Watch for a year where marketers find new work
Start a part-time sports coaching qualification in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready by then, for firms, government or people like me. I'd say it to the lads, and maybe on the football club page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I've got most of a decade in pet food marketing, if I shift toward the shops and the buyers. The AI will take over the desk side long before 2036, but I can see a path. And I'd have coaching as a back-up by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Rob to move me toward field sales over the next couple of years. I'd learn the AI tools well enough to let them do the paperwork. I'd do a coaching badge at weekends, slowly, and save a little every month once the car's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'm sleeping okay in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you save for, once the car's paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deposit, eventually. It's a long way off on my pay. But ten years feels like enough time to get somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're sleeping okay. What would wake you up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pet food firm I work for got bought by a big group, all the plans about the field side go out the window. Big groups have their own people. That would be a bad week.

say: I'd say there's **no excuse** not to be ready by 2036.
I'd say it to friends and on the **football club** page.
think: I think I've got **most of a decade** if I shift to the shops.
Coaching would be a **back-up** by the time AGI arrives.
do: Ask Rob to move me toward **field sales** over two years.
Learn the **AI tools** to handle the paperwork.
Do a **coaching badge** at weekends and save monthly.
S4.quote: If the pet food firm I work for got bought by a big group, all the plans about the field side go out the window.
fieldNote: A decade lets him see a **path** through field sales.
His fear shifts to a **takeover**, not AI itself.
He plans **slowly** and steadily, like his nature.

steps.text: Ask Rob to move him into field sales over two years
Use AI tools to handle the brochure and deal paperwork
Do a weekend football coaching badge
Save monthly toward a deposit once the car's paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time and I've got a car loan and three weeks of money. What would help is some kind of bridge, money for six months or so, so you're not forced into the first job going.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what keeps people sane. For me it's Saturday football. If you lose your job and your routine, you need something that makes you get up.

headlineQuote: If you lose your job and your routine, you need something that makes you get up.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old marketer** at a pet food brand, living alone with a car loan.
He uses AI **now and then**, once he's seen it work.
He's pragmatic and centrist, and **blames no one** in particular.
His mood runs from **uneasy** in the calm and slow pictures to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
He sees **shop visits** and Saturday football coaching as his human edge.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with a car loan and three weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **six-month bridge** of money so he isn't forced into the first job.
